s: Amphipolis was the place where Brasidas encamped with his army and met Cleon's advancing Athenians. A battle was fought there in which both generals were killed and the Lacedaemonians won.

l: the Peloponnesian War, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, In Asia, Xerxes the Persian king died, after lie had reigned one
s: The Peloponnesian War had continued for ten years before the Athenians and Lacedaemonians made peace. The settlement required prisoners on both sides to be discharged and cities taken during the war to be restored.

s: The battle of Amphipolis was fought between the Athenians under Cleon and the Lacedaemonians under Brasidas. Both generals were killed, the Lacedaemonians won, and the Athenians buried their dead under a truce.

l: the siege of Scione, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, In Asia, Xerxes the Persian king died, after lie had reigned one
s: The siege of Scione began when Nicias and Nicostratus surrounded the city with a wall and repeatedly assaulted it. Scione's strong garrison, well supplied with necessities, defended the city and inflicted heavy losses on the besiegers.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAR VIIL
s: The unit describes renewed conflict during the Peloponnesian War after Athens and Sparta formed a private league, prompting Argos, Thebes, Corinth, and Elis to organize against them. It recounts the struggle between the Argives and Lacedaemonians, including the Battle of Mantinea, the Argive oligarchic coup, and the subsequent restoration of democracy. It also reports Roman war against the Fidenates, conflicts involving the Egestaeans and Selinuntines in Sicily, and Athenian operations under Nicias. The unit concludes with the Athenian decision to send an expedition to Sicily under Alcibiades, Nicias, and Lamachus against the Syracusans.

l: the Peloponnesian War, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAR VIIL
s: The Peloponnesian War continued into its sixteenth year amid renewed conflict between Athens and Sparta and their shifting alliances. The unit ends as the Athenians prepare to pursue the war against the Syracusans in Sicily.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAR VIIL
s: The Athenians formed a private offensive and defensive league with the Spartans, created ten magistrates with broad authority, and later allied with Argos. They fought in several operations, took Cithera and Nicaea, stormed Melus, supported Argos against Ornea, and dispatched a large expedition to Sicily.

l: Lacedaemonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAR VIIL
s: The Lacedaemonians restored privileges to citizens captured at Sphacteria, freed a thousand Helots who had served with Brasidas, and sought to strengthen their alliances. They fought Argos, won the Battle of Mantinea, compelled Mantinea to submit, and later invaded Argia.

l: Spartans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAR VIIL
s: The Spartans entered a private league with the Athenians, causing other Greek cities to suspect that the two powers intended to enslave Greece. They later joined with Argos and received Corinth back into their association.

l: Argives, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAR VIIL
s: The Argives led the coalition against the Lacedaemonians and formed an alliance with the Athenians. They fought in Arcadia, captured Orchomenum, suffered defeat at Mantinea, and later restored their democracy after an oligarchic seizure of power.

l: Argos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAR VIIL
s: Argos was selected to command the coalition opposed to Athens and Sparta because of its ancient reputation, wealth, population, and long peace. It organized a thousand elite soldiers, fought Sparta, experienced an oligarchic coup, and was later supported by Alcibiades and the Athenians.

l: Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAR VIIL
s: Athens participated in the renewed struggle with Sparta and allied with Argos. Its assembly approved an expedition to Sicily after hearing appeals from the Leontines and Egestaeans, despite Nicias's opposition.

l: Sparta, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAR VIIL
s: Sparta was viewed as weakened by the capture of many prominent citizens at Sphacteria, but it reorganized its forces and defeated the Argives and their allies at Mantinea. It subsequently invaded Argia and supported the Argive exiles at Ornea.

l: Greece, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAR VIIL
s: Several Greek cities feared that the private league of Athens and Sparta aimed to dominate all Greece. Argos, Thebes, Corinth, and Elis therefore formed a counter-alliance to defend what they regarded as the common liberty.

l: Peloponnesus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAR VIIL
s: Many cities in Peloponnesus conspired against the Lacedaemonians and placed the direction of the war in Argos. The region then became divided by shifting alliances, fighting between Argos and Sparta, and political upheaval.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAR VIIL
s: Sicily was the setting of the dispute between the Egestaeans and Selinuntines and became the destination of the Athenian expedition. Nicias argued that Athens could not both fight Sparta and conquer the most powerful island in the world.

l: Rome, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAR VIIL
s: Rome declared war on the Fidenates after they killed Roman ambassadors. It appointed Manius Aemilius dictator, with Aulus Cornelius as master of the horse, and fought the Fidenates to an indecisive engagement.

l: Romans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAR VIIL
s: The Romans were angered when the Fidenates put their ambassadors to death and voted to avenge the act by war. Their forces fought the Fidenates after Manius Aemilius was appointed dictator.

l: Agis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAR VIIL
s: Agis commanded the Lacedaemonians against Argos and offered battle near the city, but a four-month truce prevented the engagement. Afterward, the Lacedaemonians nearly put him to death, spared him after his promise of future success, and assigned ten advisers to supervise his decisions.

l: Nicias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAR VIIL
s: Nicias commanded Athenian operations that captured Cithera and Nicaea and stormed Melus. He opposed the expedition to Sicily, warning that Athens could not safely fight Sparta while attempting to conquer Sicily, but he was appointed one of its three generals.

l: Alcibiades, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAR VIIL
s: Alcibiades supported the Argives and joined the Athenian force sent to them, although he held no command at that time. He later restored democracy at Argos by banishing those who favored the Lacedaemonians and was appointed one of the three generals of the expedition to Sicily.

l: Argive thousand, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAR VIIL
s: The Argive thousand were selected, well-funded soldiers trained continuously in military discipline. They fought notably at Mantinea, where they first routed part of the opposing army, and later seized power in Argos and established an oligarchy before being overthrown by a popular insurrection.

l: Egestaeans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAR VIIL
s: The Egestaeans fought the Selinuntines over disputed boundaries and were defeated with heavy losses. After failing to obtain aid from Agrigentum, Syracuse, and Carthage, they appealed to Athens and displayed borrowed and private wealth to persuade the Athenians to intervene.

l: Selinuntines, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAR VIIL
s: The Selinuntines crossed the river marking their boundary with the Egestaeans and seized neighboring lands. They defeated the Egestaeans in battle, prompting the latter to seek outside assistance.

l: Syracusans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAR VIIL
s: The Syracusans had expelled the Leontines from their city and country and refused to assist the Egestaeans. They became the principal target of the Athenian expedition to Sicily.

l: Leontines, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAR VIIL
s: The Leontines, driven out by the Syracusans, sought an alliance with Athens on the basis of their claimed descent from the Athenians. They sent ambassadors requesting help for oppressed cities and promising to support Athenian interests in Sicily.

l: Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAR VIIL
s: Syracuse was associated with the defeat and expulsion of the Leontines and declined the Egestaeans' request for aid. Its people were among those the Athenians intended to oppose in Sicily.

l: Mantinea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAR VIIL
s: Mantinea supported the Argives and faced the advancing Lacedaemonians with the youth of its city and allied forces. After the Lacedaemonians' victory, Mantinea was left without the Argive garrison and was forced under Lacedaemonian power.

l: Battle of Mantinea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAR VIIL
s: At the Battle of Mantinea, the Argive thousand initially routed part of the opposing army, but the Lacedaemonians turned against them and surrounded them. Pharax ordered a passage opened, allowing the thousand Argive soldiers to escape, while the Lacedaemonians secured the victory.

l: Argive oligarchic coup, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAR VIIL
s: The Argive thousand and their wealthy supporters overthrew the popular government, killed leading advocates of democracy, and ruled for eight months. A popular insurrection then deposed them and restored democracy.

l: Athenian expedition to Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAR VIIL
s: The Athenians approved an expedition to Sicily after hearing appeals from the Leontines and Egestaeans. They assembled 130 ships, 5,000 armed men, and the generals Alcibiades, Nicias, and Lamachus to oppose the Syracusans.

l: democracy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAR VIIL
s: Democracy in Argos was overthrown by the Argive thousand and their supporters. It was restored after a popular insurrection and later reinforced when Alcibiades banished those who favored the Lacedaemonians.

l: aristocracy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAR VIIL
s: An aristocracy was established in Argos by the Argive thousand after they seized the leading supporters of popular government. The arrangement lasted eight months before the people deposed its leaders and restored democracy.

l: league of Athens and Sparta, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAR VIIL
s: Athens and Sparta privately formed a league that was both offensive and defensive, excluding the cities that had supported either side. Its provision allowing them to add to or remove from the agreed terms led other Greek cities to suspect plans for domination and to form a counter-alliance.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. CHAP. I.
s: The Athenians prepare a large expedition against Syracuse, sending a fleet, army, and the generals Alcibiades, Nicias, and Lamachus to Sicily. After Alcibiades is accused in Athens of conspiring against the democracy, he escapes from Sicily to Sparta and persuades the Lacedaemonians to assist the Syracusans. The Athenians seize Epipolae and besiege Syracuse, but Gylippus arrives with reinforcements, Lamachus is killed, and the Syracusans recover important positions. Athens sends further aid, while Lacedaemon breaks its league with Athens and renews the war.

l: Alcibiades, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. CHAP. I.
s: Alcibiades was appointed one of three Athenian generals for the expedition against Syracuse. After being accused at Athens in connection with the mutilation of the statues of Minerva, he escaped from Sicily to Sparta, where he persuaded the Lacedaemonians to invade the Athenians and aid Syracuse.

l: Nicias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. CHAP. I.
s: Nicias served as an Athenian general in the expedition and later remained in command after Alcibiades fled and Lamachus was killed. He requested additional ships, money, and a colleague from Athens because the Syracusans had been reinforced and were preparing a fleet.

l: Lamac​hus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. CHAP. I.
s: Lamachus was one of the three Athenian generals sent against Syracuse. He was killed in a battle with the forces of Gylippus and the Syracusans.

l: Gylippus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. CHAP. I.
s: Gylippus was appointed general by the Lacedaemonians to aid Syracuse. He raised troops at Himera and elsewhere in Sicily, entered Syracuse with reinforcements, and led the Syracusans against the Athenians, helping them recover the fortifications at Epipolae.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. CHAP. I.
s: The Athenians decreed war against the Syracusans, equipped a major fleet, raised troops, and sent the expedition to Sicily. They captured Catana, seized Epipolae, built fortifications around Syracuse, defeated the Syracusans in several engagements, and later requested and received additional money, ships, and cavalry.

l: Syracusans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. CHAP. I.
s: The Syracusans appointed Hermocrates, Sicanus, and Heraclides as generals and sought aid from Corinth and Lacedaemon. They resisted the Athenian siege, received Gylippus and other reinforcements, defeated the Athenians at Epipolae, and prepared a fleet for a sea-fight.

l: Lacedaemonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. CHAP. I.
s: The Lacedaemonians agreed, at the urging of Alcibiades, to assist the Syracusans and appointed Gylippus as general. They later sent six hundred men to Syracuse and broke their league with the Athenians.

l: Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. CHAP. I.
s: Athens prepared the expedition against Syracuse and condemned Alcibiades to death after he fled. It later voted to send three hundred talents, cavalry, ships, money, and additional forces to support the war in Sicily.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. CHAP. I.
s: Sicily was the target of the Athenian expedition, although the Syracusans warned that Athens intended to subdue the whole island. Several Sicilian cities supported, resisted, or remained neutral toward the Athenians, while Gylippus recruited troops across the island for Syracuse.

l: Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. CHAP. I.
s: Syracuse was besieged by the Athenians after they seized Epipolae and fortified positions near its port. The city received aid from Gylippus, Corinth, and Lacedaemon, and its forces eventually demolished the Athenian walls and fortifications at Epipolae.

l: Sparta, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. CHAP. I.
s: Sparta received Alcibiades after his flight from Sicily. There he persuaded the Lacedaemonians to invade the Athenians and aid Syracuse.

l: Lacedaemon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. CHAP. I.
s: Lacedaemon was asked by Syracuse to provide aid and sent Gylippus, followed by additional troops. At the instigation of Alcibiades, it broke its league with Athens, beginning a renewed war.

l: Epipolae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. CHAP. I.
s: Epipolae was seized by the Athenians in a night attack and became part of their fortified position around Syracuse. Gylippus and the Syracusans later assaulted it, defeated the Athenians, and demolished its walls and fortifications.

l: Athenian expedition to Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. CHAP. I.
s: The Athenian expedition was commanded by Alcibiades, Nicias, and Lamachus and included more than seven thousand armed men, along with a large fleet. It moved from Athens through Corcyra and Italy to Sicily, where it captured Hyccara, occupied Catana, and began operations against Syracuse.

l: Alcibiades's flight from Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. CHAP. I.
s: After Athens recalled Alcibiades to stand trial, he sailed from Catana but escaped at Thurii. He then fled from Italy to Sparta, while Athens condemned him and his fellow fugitives to death in their absence.

l: Athenians' Sicilian expedition, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. CHAP. I.
s: The Athenians seized Epipolae, fortified Labdalon and Polichna, and built walls that blocked Syracuse and its port. The siege was weakened when Gylippus arrived with reinforcements and the Syracusans destroyed the Athenian fortifications at Epipolae.

l: battle at Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. CHAP. I.
s: The forces of Gylippus and the Syracusans fought the Athenians near Syracuse, and Lamachus was killed. Although the Athenians initially won the battle, the Syracusans later defeated them in an assault on the Athenian camp and Epipolae.

l: war between Lacedaemon and Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. CHAP. I.
s: At the instigation of Alcibiades, the Lacedaemonians broke their league with Athens. The text states that the war between them continued for twelve years.

l: Athenian fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. CHAP. I.
s: The Athenians equipped 140 galleys, in addition to ships for horses, provisions, and other necessities, for the expedition. The fleet sailed through the Ionian Sea and along the Italian coast to Sicily, later moved from Catana to the great port of Syracuse, and received further support from Athens.

l: Athenian army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. CHAP. I.
s: The Athenian army included more than seven thousand armed men, slingers, and cavalry from the allied forces. It captured Hyccara, fought the Syracusans, occupied Epipolae, built siege works around Syracuse, and later withdrew to another position after losing Epipolae.

l: Syracusan officers, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS. .. CHAP. I.
s: The Syracusan army was organized under Hermocrates, Sicanus, and Heraclides and fought the invading Athenians. It received reinforcements from Gylippus and other allies, defeated the Athenians at Epipolae, and helped demolish their walls and fortifications.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. II.
s: The Lacedemonians invaded Attica under Agis and fortified Decelea, while the Athenians sent forces toward Laconia and Sicily. The Syracusans and Athenians fought a sea-fight in which the Athenians initially sank eleven Syracusan ships but also lost their forts on land. After Demosthenes was expected to arrive with a fleet, the Syracusans provoked another battle in the Great Haven and defeated the Athenians, sinking seven of their galleys and disabling many more. The Syracusans benefited from stronger, lower-built forecastles, while the Athenians were hindered by the narrow fighting space.

l: Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. II.
s: Athens was governed by Cleocritus during this year. It sent Chares with thirty sail into Laconia and decreed that eighty galleys and five thousand soldiers be sent into Sicily.

l: Lacedaemonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. II.
s: The Lacedemonians invaded Attica under Agis as their general. They seized Decelea and built a fort there.

l: Attica, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. II.
s: Attica was invaded by the Lacedemonians under Agis.

l: Decelea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. II.
s: Decelea was a strong place suitable for a garrison. The Lacedemonians seized it and built a fort there, giving the war its name.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. II.
s: The Athenians decreed that eighty galleys and five thousand soldiers be sent into Sicily. The fighting described in this unit took place between the Athenians and Syracusans in Sicily.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. II.
s: The Athenians fought the Syracusans by sea, initially sinking eleven Syracusan ships, but they also lost two forts and suffered a later defeat in the Great Haven. Their galleys were faster and their sailors more skilled, but the narrow waters deprived them of these advantages; seven of their galleys were sunk and many more disabled.

l: Syracusans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. II.
s: The Syracusans used a diversion to seize the lightly guarded Athenian forts while the main fleets fought at sea. They later defeated the Athenians in the Great Haven, sinking seven galleys and disabling many more.

l: sea-fight, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. II.
s: The first sea-fight involved eighty well-manned Syracusan ships and sixty Athenian ships; the Athenians sank eleven Syracusan ships after turning back to fight. A later sea-fight in the Great Haven favored the Syracusans, who used their stronger, lower forecastles to board and defeat the Athenian galleys.

l: fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. II.
s: The Athenians delayed further action while awaiting Demosthenes with a fleet. The Syracusans repeatedly challenged the Athenian fleet and eventually engaged it fully in the Great Haven.

l: gallies, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. II.
s: The Athenians were assigned eighty galleys for the Sicilian expedition, and sixty took part in the first sea-fight. Their galleys were swift but had slender, high-built forecastles, while the Syracusan vessels had low, strongly built foredecks that could damage them at the first strike.

l: Athenian forts, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. II.
s: The Athenian forts contained money, naval preparations, and other provisions. They were lightly guarded and were seized by the Syracusans while the Athenians were drawn toward the sea-fight.

l: Demosthenes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. II.
s: Demosthenes was expected to arrive within a few days with a fleet and additional forces. The Athenians resolved to attempt nothing further until his forces arrived.

s: Eurymedon and Demosthenes arrived in Sicily with a large Athenian force, but a night assault on Epipolae failed after the Syracusans rallied under Hermocrates. The plague and the arrival of further Syracusan aid weakened the Athenians, while a lunar eclipse delayed their planned departure. The Athenians then lost successive naval engagements in Syracuse harbor, abandoned their ships, and retreated by land, where the Syracusans defeated and captured them.

l: Eurymedon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, t)otb by sea and land, presently arrive Gurymedovand Demostlieiio,
s: Eurymedon arrived with Demosthenes and a large army from Athens, together with additional forces from Tholium and Messapia. He commanded the Athenian right wing in the first naval battle in Syracuse harbor, where he was mortally wounded and killed, and seven ships under his command were destroyed.

l: Demosthenes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, t)otb by sea and land, presently arrive Gurymedovand Demostlieiio,
s: Demosthenes arrived in Sicily with Eurymedon and substantial reinforcements. He persuaded his colleagues to attack Epipolae, later urged an immediate return to Athens, and after the naval defeat proposed manning more ships to force the harbor blockade; he was captured during the retreat.

l: Nicias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, t)otb by sea and land, presently arrive Gurymedovand Demostlieiio,
s: Nicias opposed abandoning the siege because the Athenians still possessed ships, men, and money and might be blamed for leaving without orders from the people. He eventually accepted the retreat, delayed it after the lunar eclipse on the advice of soothsayers, and was captured with Demosthenes after the army was defeated.

l: Hermocrates, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, t)otb by sea and land, presently arrive Gurymedovand Demostlieiio,
s: Hermocrates led a choice band of young men to aid the Syracusans during the night assault on Epipolae, helping drive the Athenians out. He later advised drawing out the Syracusan forces at night and blocking the roads, but the officers rejected his advice.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, t)otb by sea and land, presently arrive Gurymedovand Demostlieiio,
s: The Athenians arrived with a large army and attempted to seize Epipolae, but suffered heavy losses in the failed assault. Plague, naval defeats, and the loss of their escape route forced them to retreat by land, where many were killed and the survivors were captured.

l: Syracusans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, t)otb by sea and land, presently arrive Gurymedovand Demostlieiio,
s: The Syracusans rallied against the Athenian assault on Epipolae, obtained aid from neighboring cities, and defeated the Athenians in naval engagements. They blocked the harbor, destroyed or disabled many Athenian ships, pursued the retreating army, and captured seven thousand prisoners after killing eighteen thousand.

l: Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, t)otb by sea and land, presently arrive Gurymedovand Demostlieiio,
s: Syracuse was threatened by the Athenian siege but became encouraged by reinforcements and victories on land and sea. The city ultimately secured its safety, celebrated the defeat of the Athenians, erected two trophies, and gave public thanks to the gods.

l: Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, t)otb by sea and land, presently arrive Gurymedovand Demostlieiio,
s: Athens was the home of the Athenian forces, and Demosthenes argued that it was more commendable to risk their lives for Athens against the Lacedaemonians than to remain inactive in Sicily. Nicias feared criticism at Athens if the generals abandoned the siege without authorization from the people.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, t)otb by sea and land, presently arrive Gurymedovand Demostlieiio,
s: Sicily was the location of the Athenian campaign, the plague-stricken army, the naval battles, and the final retreat. The Athenians intended to leave Sicily and march toward cities of their confederates, but were intercepted and defeated.

l: Epipolae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, t)otb by sea and land, presently arrive Gurymedovand Demostlieiio,
s: Epipolae was the high position that Demosthenes believed the Athenians had to seize in order to surround and pressure Syracuse. The Athenians attacked it at night, briefly took some forts, entered the fortifications, and demolished part of the wall before being driven out.

l: Athenians' Sicilian expedition, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, t)otb by sea and land, presently arrive Gurymedovand Demostlieiio,
s: The expedition received reinforcements but then declined because of the failed assault, the plague, Syracusan aid, and naval defeats. Its remaining forces abandoned the fleet and attempted a land retreat, ending with the deaths of eighteen thousand men and the capture of seven thousand.

l: Athenian night assault on Epipolae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, t)otb by sea and land, presently arrive Gurymedovand Demostlieiio,
s: The Athenians attacked Epipolae unexpectedly at night with ten thousand heavy-armed and an equal number of light-armed troops. They took forts and damaged the wall, but darkness and unfamiliarity with the passages caused their dispersion, and the Syracusans killed two thousand five hundred and wounded many more.

l: plague in the Athenian camp, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, t)otb by sea and land, presently arrive Gurymedovand Demostlieiio,
s: The plague broke out in the Athenian army because of a stinking marshy area nearby. It spread and killed a large part of the army, causing the Athenians to regret that they had not departed earlier.

l: lunar eclipse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, t)otb by sea and land, presently arrive Gurymedovand Demostlieiio,
s: A lunar eclipse occurred on the night before the Athenians intended to sail. Nicias, who was superstitious and distressed by the plague, consulted soothsayers, who advised delaying the departure for three days.

l: first naval battle in Syracuse harbor, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, t)otb by sea and land, presently arrive Gurymedovand Demostlieiio,

s: The Lacedaemonians supported oligarchies among their allies and fought Athens at Dardanium, Cyzicum, and Claros. Their fleet fled at Dardanium, and their army and fleet were decisively defeated at Claros.

l: Thrasybulus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Thrasybulus commanded the Athenian right wing at Dardanium. At Claros he attacked the enemy's land support, initially endured heavy pressure, and later received Theramenes's assistance before the combined Athenian forces prevailed.

l: Pharnabazus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Pharnabazus supported the Lacedaemonian fleet with land forces at Dardanium and assisted Mindarus in capturing Cyzicum. At Claros his army fought from the shore, but it was eventually broken and withdrew with the Peloponnesians.

l: Theramenes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Theramenes attempted to stop the Boeotians from blocking the Euripus but withdrew when overpowered. He later helped restore democracy at Paros and, at Claros, joined Chares's infantry to reinforce Thrasybulus and defeat the enemy on land.

l: Corcyra, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Corcyra experienced a violent political conflict between supporters of oligarchy and democracy. The democrats sought Athenian assistance, expelled many oligarchic supporters, and later reached a settlement granting equal privileges.

l: Corcyrian sedition, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: The Corcyrian sedition arose from private grudges and the struggle between oligarchic supporters of the Lacedaemonians and democrats favoring Athens. The democrats killed or imprisoned opponents and expelled more than a thousand, but a later armed clash ended in pacification.

l: oligarchy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Oligarchy was favored by the Lacedaemonians and by the leading men at Corcyra who sought to bring the city under Lacedaemonian control. Theramenes removed an oligarchy at Paros and restored the democracy.

l: the Athenian democracy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Democracy was promoted by Athens in its allied cities and supported by the people of Corcyra. The democratic faction at Corcyra expelled its oligarchic opponents, while Theramenes restored democratic government at Paros.

l: Cyzicum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Cyzicum was besieged and captured by Mindarus with assistance from Pharnabazus. The Athenians then sailed there, trapped the Peloponnesian fleet, and fought the decisive battle that led to the death of Mindarus.

l: Battle of Cyzicum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: In the Battle of Cyzicum, Alcibiades drew Mindarus's ships away from the city while Theramenes and Thrasybulus blocked their return. The Athenians defeated the Peloponnesians, captured many ships and prisoners, and gained abundant spoils.

l: Alcibiades, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Alcibiades unexpectedly joined the battle at Dardanium with twenty ships and signaled the Athenians with a purple flag, causing the Lacedaemonians to flee. At Cyzicum he used a feigned flight to lure Mindarus away from the city, then attacked and pursued him to Claros.

l: Claros, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Claros was the coastal place where Mindarus fled after being cut off from Cyzicum. Pharnabazus's army was encamped there and supported the Peloponnesians against the Athenians.

l: Battle of Claros, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: The Battle of Claros began when the Athenians tried to seize Peloponnesian ships forced onto the shore. After Theramenes joined Thrasybulus and the Persian forces broke, Mindarus was killed and the Peloponnesians fled.

l: Athenian fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: The Athenian fleet numbered seventy-four ships at Dardanium and defeated the opposing fleet after Alcibiades arrived. It later assembled at Sestos and Cardia, sailed to Cyzicum, and captured the enemy ships after the victories at sea and land.

l: Peloponnesian fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: The Peloponnesian fleet fought the Athenians at Dardanium under Mindarus and later assembled for operations from Abydos. It was drawn away from Cyzicum, defeated at sea and on land, and largely captured or driven off.

l: Pharnabazus's army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. V.
s: Pharnabazus's army supported the Peloponnesians at Dardanium and Claros. At Claros it fought from the shore and initially inflicted heavy losses on the Athenians, but it eventually broke and withdrew.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: After learning of their rout at Cyzicum, the Spartans sent ambassadors to Athens to negotiate peace, with Endius as their chief representative. Endius proposed retaining the cities each side had gained, dismissing all garrisons, and exchanging prisoners one Athenian for one Lacedaemonian. He argued that the war harmed both sides but weakened the Athenians more, while also appealing to the Spartans' customary concern about bloodshed. Although moderate Athenians favored peace, Cleophon persuaded the assembly to reject it by magnifying the Athenians' recent victories, and the Athenians remained confident that they would soon recover their former reputation.

l: Spartans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: After receiving certain intelligence of their rout at Cyzicum, the Spartans sent ambassadors to Athens to negotiate peace. They sought an end to the war while arguing that the Athenians had suffered more severely.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: The Athenians received the Spartan ambassadors but refused the proposed peace. They were encouraged by their recent victories and believed that Alcibiades's leadership would help them recover their former esteem and reputation.

l: Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Athens was the destination of the Spartan peace embassy. Its assembly heard Endius's proposals, but the Athenians ultimately rejected them.

l: Endius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Endius led the Spartan embassy to Athens and delivered a brief, pointed speech. He argued that the war was more damaging to the Athenians and presented the Spartan conditions for peace.

l: Cleophon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Cleophon opposed the peace proposal in the Athenian assembly. He magnified the Athenians' recent successes and urged them to believe that fortune would not reverse their gains.

l: Cyzicum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: Cyzicum was the place associated with the Spartans' rout, news of which prompted them to send ambassadors to Athens.

l: the Peloponnesian War, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: The war had brought many confederates to the Laconians while the Athenians had lost as many as the Laconians gained. It had also caused murders and extensive bloodshed, and Endius argued that continuing it would harm both sides.

l: peace, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: The Spartans sought peace with Athens, but the Athenians refused after Cleophon encouraged confidence in their recent successes.

l: the rout at Cyzicum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: The rout at Cyzicum was confirmed to the Spartans and led them to send an embassy to Athens seeking peace.

l: the peace terms, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: The proposed peace terms allowed each side to retain the cities it had gained, required the dismissal of all garrisons, and called for the release of prisoners at a rate of one Athenian for one Lacedaemonian.

l: the Athenians' victories, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VI.
s: The Athenians' recent victories were emphasized by Cleophon, who used them to encourage rejection of peace. The Athenians consequently became confident that they would soon recover their former esteem and reputation.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Hannibal led a large Carthaginian army from Spain and Africa to Sicily, captured Selinus after a prolonged siege, and destroyed the city. The Syracusans and other Sicilian allies prepared to aid Selinus but arrived too late, while Agrigentum received thousands of Selinuntine refugees. Hannibal then besieged and captured Himera, defeating its defenders and destroying the city after the Syracusan forces withdrew. He returned to Carthage with prisoners and abundant booty, and the people received him with great acclaim.

l: Hannibal, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Hannibal led the Carthaginian invasion of Sicily with a large army and fleet. He captured and destroyed Selinus, then besieged and destroyed Himera, ordered prisoners and temples treated according to his stated purposes, and finally returned to Carthage with abundant booty.

l: Carthaginians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: The Carthaginians invaded Sicily, captured Selinus after nine days of assaults, and killed or enslaved many of its inhabitants. They later defeated the Himerians, captured and destroyed Himera, and returned to Carthage with prisoners and plunder.

l: Selinuntines, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: The Selinuntines resisted Hannibal's army with all their available forces, aided by women and children who carried food and weapons and defended the streets with stones and tiles. After repeated assaults and the loss of their walls, they were overwhelmed; sixteen thousand were killed, more than five thousand were carried away captive, and about twenty-five hundred escaped to Agrigentum.

l: Syracusans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: The Syracusans made peace with the Chalcidonians and gathered forces to aid Selinus, but they delayed because they did not believe the city was in immediate danger. They later sent four thousand men under Diodes to aid Himera, but withdrew when Hannibal's fleet threatened Syracuse.

l: Himerians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: The Himerians defended their city against Hannibal and received assistance from four thousand Syracusans and other allies. They made a successful sortie against the Carthaginians but were eventually defeated after the Syracusan forces withdrew, and Himera was captured and destroyed.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Sicily was invaded by Hannibal and the Carthaginian army, which captured and destroyed Selinus and Himera. Several Sicilian cities considered or provided aid to the besieged, while Hannibal eventually departed with his army and booty.

l: Selinus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Selinus was besieged and captured by Hannibal after its defenders held out against repeated assaults. The city was burned, demolished, and depopulated, although Hannibal later permitted refugees to return and cultivate its lands under Carthaginian tribute.

l: Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Syracuse was asked to aid Selinus and began gathering forces after making peace with the Chalcidonians. Hannibal later planned to sail against Syracuse with selected troops, believing it lacked sufficient strength to defend itself, but the intended attack did not occur in this unit.

l: Himera, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Himera was besieged by Hannibal after the destruction of Selinus. Although its defenders initially repelled the Carthaginians and killed many of them, the city was eventually entered, plundered, burned, and razed to the ground.

l: Carthage, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Carthage received Hannibal after his campaign in Sicily. Its people came out to meet him and celebrated him as a general who had accomplished exceptionally great deeds in a short time.

l: the siege of Selinus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: The siege began after Hannibal landed in Sicily and marched from Lilybaeum toward Selinus. Hannibal used towers, battering rams, archers, and fresh troops in repeated assaults until breaches were opened and the Carthaginians captured the city.

l: the fall and destruction of Selinus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: After Selinus fell, the Carthaginians killed inhabitants, plundered houses, burned or demolished buildings, and destroyed the city. Sixteen thousand people were killed and more than five thousand were taken captive, while Agrigentum received about twenty-five hundred refugees.

l: destruction of Himera, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Hannibal besieged Himera with Carthaginian and Sicilian forces, battering and undermining its walls. After the defenders were defeated and the city was entered, Hannibal ordered the inhabitants' slaughter to stop, but the city was plundered, its temples were burned, and Himera was razed.

l: the Battle of Himera, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: The Himerians and their allies made a sudden sortie against the Carthaginian army and initially routed it, killing thousands. Hannibal brought reinforcements from the camp, defeated the Himerians in a second engagement, and three thousand Himerians died after making a determined stand.

l: the Carthaginian invasion of Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Hannibal began the Carthaginian invasion of Sicily by bringing an army from Spain and Africa aboard warships and transports. The invasion resulted in the capture and destruction of Selinus and Himera before Hannibal withdrew to Carthage with booty.

l: the Carthaginian army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: The Carthaginian army was described by Ephorus as numbering two hundred thousand foot and four thousand horse, while Timaeus gave a much smaller figure. It used siege towers, battering rams, archers, and fresh troops to overcome Selinus and Himera.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, At this timie Hermocrates the Syracusan returned intoSicilji He
s: Hermocrates the Syracusan, banished by the Syracusans, raised troops and attacked Carthaginian territories in Sicily, gaining high esteem among the Sicilians. The Syracusans regretted his banishment and began showing support for his recall. In Greece, Thrasybulus failed to take Ephesus, while the Athenians conducted operations around Chalcedon, Pylos, and Byzantium. Alcibiades and Theramenes ultimately captured Byzantium after a betrayal by some of its inhabitants.

l: Hermocrates, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, At this timie Hermocrates the Syracusan returned intoSicilji He
s: Hermocrates the Syracusan was highly esteemed among the Syracusans for his service in the war against the Athenians. After being banished, he received money from Pharnabazus, built galleys at Messana, hired soldiers, and gathered a force of six thousand men at Selinus. He raided Motya, Panormus, and other territories subject to the Carthaginians, winning high esteem among the Sicilians and seeking to return to Syracuse.

l: Syracusans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, At this timie Hermocrates the Syracusan returned intoSicilji He
s: The Syracusans had Hermocrates condemned to banishment through a contrary faction. After hearing of his successes against the Carthaginians, they regretted the decision and gave signs in public assemblies that they wanted him recalled.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, At this timie Hermocrates the Syracusan returned intoSicilji He
s: Sicily was the setting for Hermocrates's activities after his banishment. Hermocrates attacked territories subject to the Carthaginians, while the Syracusans reconsidered his banishment.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, At this timie Hermocrates the Syracusan returned intoSicilji He
s: The Athenians operated with fleets and armies around Ephesus, Chalcedon, Pylos, and Byzantium. They defeated the Megareans near the hill called the Florus, besieged and captured Byzantium, and restored the city to the Byzantines.

l: Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, At this timie Hermocrates the Syracusan returned intoSicilji He
s: Athens sent forces to relieve the besieged at Pylos and later sent forces against the Megareans after Nicaea was taken. The people of Athens condemned Anytus to death after he failed to reach Pylos, though he redeemed his life with money.

l: Lacedaemonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, At this timie Hermocrates the Syracusan returned intoSicilji He
s: The Lacedaemonians besieged Pylos by land and sea, but the Messenians there eventually surrendered. They also held Chalcedon and Byzantium with garrisons, though their forces were defeated or expelled from both places.

l: Thrasybulus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, At this timie Hermocrates the Syracusan returned intoSicilji He
s: Thrasybulus sailed from Athens with thirty ships and an army and assaulted Ephesus, but the townsmen drove him back after killing four hundred Athenians. He later brought cities in Thrace under the power of the Athenians and joined Alcibiades and Theramenes in the operations against Byzantium.

l: Chalcedon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, At this timie Hermocrates the Syracusan returned intoSicilji He
s: Chalcedon was besieged by Theramenes with an Athenian force. After Hippocrates was killed in a sortie, Theramenes reached an agreement with the Chalcedonians that they would pay the same tribute as before.

l: Alcibiades, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, At this timie Hermocrates the Syracusan returned intoSicilji He
s: Alcibiades led Athenian operations in the region of Pharnabazus, gathered money and Thracian support, and took Selymbria by surrender. He then joined Theramenes in attacking Byzantium and captured it after promising that none of the Byzantines would be harmed.

l: Pylos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, At this timie Hermocrates the Syracusan returned intoSicilji He
s: Pylos was besieged by the Lacedaemonians, who attacked it by land and sea. The Messenians in its garrison eventually surrendered because of losses and lack of provisions, and Pylos passed into Lacedaemonian hands after the Athenians had held it for fifteen years.

l: Byzantium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, At this timie Hermocrates the Syracusan returned intoSicilji He
s: Byzantium was besieged by Theramenes and later attacked jointly by Theramenes and Alcibiades. Some Byzantines betrayed the city, allowing the Athenians to enter, after which the city was restored to the Byzantines and its league with the Athenians was renewed.

l: Theramenes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, At this timie Hermocrates the Syracusan returned intoSicilji He
s: Theramenes was left with fifty ships to besiege Chalcedon and later agreed with the Chalcedonians that they would pay their former tribute. He then moved against Byzantium and joined Alcibiades in attacking the city.

l: Athenian fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, At this timie Hermocrates the Syracusan returned intoSicilji He
s: The fleet was central to the operations described in Greece, including the Athenian movements around Ephesus, Chalcedon, Pylos, and Byzantium. Fleets were also used to blockade cities, collect a tenth from shipping near Chrysopolis, and assist in the capture of Byzantium.

l: Hermocrates’s banishment, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, At this timie Hermocrates the Syracusan returned intoSicilji He
s: Hermocrates’s banishment was imposed by a contrary faction at home after he had served as admiral. It prevented his immediate return to Syracuse, but his later military successes caused the Syracusans to regret it and consider recalling him.

l: siege of Chalcedon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, At this timie Hermocrates the Syracusan returned intoSicilji He
s: The siege of Chalcedon was conducted by Theramenes with an Athenian fleet and army. The Athenians built a timber wall from sea to sea, defeated a sortie led by Hippocrates, and then reached an agreement under which Chalcedon paid its previous tribute.

l: betrayal of Byzantium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, At this timie Hermocrates the Syracusan returned intoSicilji He
s: The betrayal of Byzantium was carried out by some Byzantines who disliked Clearchus's harsh government. They helped Alcibiades's soldiers enter the city while the Peloponnesians were drawn toward the harbor, and the Athenians then took control after promising that the Byzantines would not be harmed.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IX.
s: Alcibiades returned to Athens and was restored to his property, absolved from his condemnation, and appointed commander with authority by sea and land. He defeated the Andrians but suffered a naval defeat at Notium when Antiochus disobeyed his orders and engaged Lysander. Agis attacked Athens but was repulsed, while Alcibiades later devastated Cuma and was accused by the Cumeans and others of misconduct. Athens then appointed Conon admiral, and Alcibiades surrendered the fleet and withdrew to Thrace.

l: Alcibiades, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IX.
s: Alcibiades returned to Athens amid great admiration, defended himself before the assembly, recovered his confiscated property, and was absolved from his condemnation and alleged profanation of the mysteries. He was appointed commander with full authority by sea and land, defeated the Andrians, and later suffered defeat at Notium because Antiochus disobeyed his orders. He devastated Cuma, was accused of attacking a confederate city, surrendered the fleet to Conon, and withdrew to Thrace rather than return to Athens.

l: Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IX.
s: Athens welcomed Alcibiades with great enthusiasm and restored his property and honors. It resisted Agis's attack and later became suspicious of Alcibiades, appointing ten new commanders and choosing Conon as admiral.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IX.
s: The Athenian generals gained control of nearly all the cities of the Hellespont and returned to Athens with many captured ships, prisoners, and spoils. The Athenians defeated the Andrians and repulsed Agis's attack, but lost twenty-two ships at Notium.

l: Lacedaemonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IX.
s: The Lacedaemonians appointed Lysander admiral after losing much of their fleet and control of the sea. With support from Cyrus and allied cities, they rebuilt and supplied their fleet for the war against Athens.

l: Lysander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IX.
s: Lysander was appointed admiral of the Lacedaemonians and gathered soldiers, sailors, and ships at Rhodes, Ephesus, Miletus, and Chios. He obtained financial support from Cyrus and defeated the Athenian fleet at Notium after learning that Alcibiades had sailed away.

l: Agis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IX.
s: Agis marched against Athens with a large force and initially seized two parts of the walls. The Athenians defeated his cavalry and forced him to abandon the attempt to besiege the city before he returned to Peloponnesus.

l: Conon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IX.
s: Conon was chosen from among ten newly appointed Athenian commanders to be admiral. He was sent to receive the fleet from Alcibiades and took command of it.

l: Cumaeans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IX.
s: The Cumeans defended their city and country when Alcibiades attacked and carried off prisoners. They defeated his force, recovered the captives, and brought a formal accusation against him at Athens for wasting a confederate city that had done them no injury.

l: Ephesus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IX.
s: Ephesus received Lysander, who assembled a fleet there and obtained further ships and supplies from neighboring cities. Lysander later sailed from Ephesus with seventy ships.

l: Notium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IX.
s: Notium was the place where the Athenian fleet anchored while Alcibiades went elsewhere with several ships. A naval battle occurred nearby, in which Lysander defeated the Athenians and destroyed or captured twenty-two of their ships.

l: Cuma, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IX.
s: Cuma was attacked and devastated by Alcibiades under the pretense of charges against its inhabitants. Its people defeated his force and afterward accused him at Athens of wasting a confederate city.

l: war against the Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IX.
s: The war continued with shifting fortunes at sea and on land. The Lacedaemonians rebuilt their naval power under Lysander with support from Cyrus, while the Athenians recalled Alcibiades, later removed him, and appointed Conon as admiral.

l: battle of Notium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IX.
s: The battle of Notium began when Antiochus, contrary to Alcibiades's orders, challenged the Lacedaemonians. Lysander sank Antiochus's ship, routed the remaining advance vessels, and defeated the Athenian fleet with the loss of twenty-two ships.

l: Athenian fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IX.
s: The Athenian fleet returned to Athens with about two hundred captured ships, prisoners, and rich spoils. It later suffered defeat at Notium after Antiochus engaged Lysander without waiting for Alcibiades, and Alcibiades ultimately surrendered command of it to Conon.

l: Spartan fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IX.
s: The Spartan fleet was rebuilt after losing much of its strength and its commander Mindarus. Lysander gathered ships from Rhodes, Ephesus, Miletus, and Chios, received funding from Cyrus, and used the fleet to defeat the Athenians at Notium.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. X.
s: Hermocrates sent the bodies of Syracusans killed at Himera to Syracuse, causing the people to turn against Diocles, who was banished, though Hermocrates was not restored. Hermocrates later attempted to return to Syracuse with three thousand armed men, but the Syracusans killed him and many of his accomplices; Dionysius escaped after being reported dead. Callicratides, appointed admiral by the Lacedaemonians, defeated Conon’s smaller fleet near Mitylene and besieged the city after forcing the Athenians into its inner harbour.

l: Hermocrates, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. X.
s: Hermocrates marched from Selinus to Himera, gathered the bodies of the Syracusans killed there, placed them in richly adorned chariots, and sent them to Syracuse. He later attempted to return to Syracuse with three thousand armed men, but the Syracusans killed him and many of his accomplices.

l: Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. X.
s: Syracuse received the bodies of the Syracusans killed at Himera, and its people unanimously supported their burial. The Syracusans then killed Hermocrates and many of his accomplices during his attempted return.

l: Dionysius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. X.
s: Dionysius was among those badly wounded in Hermocrates' attempted return. His friends reported him dead to protect him from the immediate fury of the people, and he later usurped the tyranny.

l: Callicratides, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. X.
s: Callicratides was appointed admiral by the Lacedaemonians and received the fleet from Lysander. He took Methymna and besieged Mitylene, defeated the Athenians in the harbour, and then surrounded the city.

l: Conon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. X.
s: Conon assembled a fleet of seventy ships and went to the aid of Methymna. He lured part of the Peloponnesian fleet into pursuit, attacked it near Mitylene, and later withdrew with forty ships into the city after the larger enemy fleet arrived.

l: Lysander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. X.
s: Lysander had previously commanded the Lacedaemonian fleet but was discharged from that command. He delivered the fleet at Ephesus to Callicratides.

l: Lacedaemonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. X.
s: The Lacedaemonians appointed Callicratides as admiral after Lysander's discharge. Their fleet under Callicratides fought the Athenians at Mitylene and later besieged the city.
